title: 3 Days Before the Wedding: Do Grandma's Home Remedies Actually Work?
description: With exactly three days until her wedding, Emma's family keeps hitting one small health hiccup after another, and every time, Grandma reaches for the same old home remedy. Emma, a nursing student, fact-checks each one on the spot. Honey and lemon, ginger, chicken soup, oatmeal, which ones actually hold up to real research, and which are just old wives' tales? Watch to the end to find out.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Does honey actually cure a sore throat?
beats.caption: Does honey cure a sore throat?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Or is that just something grandmas say?
beats.caption: Or just something grandmas say?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Three days before Emma's wedding, her family hit four health hiccups in a row.
beats.caption: 3 days, 4 health hiccups

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: I'm a nursing student, so every time Grandma hands me a remedy, I fact-check it on the spot.
beats.caption: I fact-check every single one

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Honey for a sore throat. Ginger for motion sickness. Chicken soup for a cold. Oatmeal for a rash. Four remedies. Which ones are real, and which ones aren't? Stick around to find out.
beats.caption: 4 remedies. Real or not? Stick around.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That morning, Emma woke up with a scratchy, raw throat.
beats.caption: Morning one, Emma's throat is raw

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Oh honey, your voice sounds rough. Let me make you some warm water with honey and lemon.
beats.caption: "Let me make honey and lemon"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Grandma, be honest, how does honey and lemon actually help a sore throat?
beats.caption: "How does honey actually help?"

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: I have no idea, sweetheart. My mother did it, so I kept doing it. You look it up.
beats.caption: "No idea, you look it up"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Honey produces a real antibacterial compound called hydrogen peroxide, through an enzyme reaction with moisture. That's genuinely calming to an irritated throat.
beats.caption: Honey makes real antibacterial compounds

factReveal.citation: Honey's antibacterial mechanism (glucose oxidase producing hydrogen peroxide) supports its use for wound care and throat irritation

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: So I've been doing it right this whole time? I really thought I was just guessing.
beats.caption: "So I was right this whole time?"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: One point for you, Grandma. But the next one is where it gets interesting.
beats.caption: 1 point. Next one gets interesting.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That afternoon, the family piled into the car to check out the venue.
beats.caption: That afternoon, off to the venue

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Halfway there, Emma's little cousin started looking green.
beats.caption: Halfway there, cousin turns green

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: I always keep fresh ginger in my bag for exactly this. Chew on this, sweetie.
beats.caption: "Chew this ginger, sweetie"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Does ginger actually stop motion sickness, or is it just the strong taste distracting her?
beats.caption: "Does ginger really stop it?"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Ginger contains gingerol, which blocks a gut receptor that sends nausea signals to the brain. There are real clinical trials on this.
beats.caption: Gingerol blocks nausea signals

factReveal.citation: Clinical studies on ginger extract for motion sickness prevention, mechanism via gingerol inhibiting 5-HT3 receptor activity

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: And here I thought it was just a taste thing. There's actual science behind this?
beats.caption: "Actual science behind this?"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Two for two, Grandma. But tonight's remedy is the one I've always doubted most.
beats.caption: 2/2. Tonight's is the one I doubt most.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That night, after a long day, Emma's scratchy throat turned into something worse.
beats.caption: That night, a cold sets in

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Grandma, I think I'm actually getting sick now. Stuffy, achy, all of it.
beats.caption: "I think I'm actually sick"

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Let me make you a big pot of chicken soup, just like always.
beats.caption: "Chicken soup, just like always"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: This one I've always been skeptical of. It just feels like comfort food, not medicine.
beats.caption: "Feels like comfort food, not medicine"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Researchers actually tested chicken soup against the white blood cells that cause cold symptoms, and it slowed them down. A real, measured effect.
beats.caption: Soup really does slow cold symptoms

factReveal.citation: University of Nebraska Medical Center study found chicken soup inhibits neutrophil migration, a mechanism linked to easing upper respiratory symptoms

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Three for three. My kitchen is basically a pharmacy at this point.
beats.caption: 3/3! My kitchen is a pharmacy

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: I did not expect to agree with you this much. But tomorrow is the real test.
beats.caption: Tomorrow is the real test

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Wedding morning. During the final fitting, Emma's arm broke out in an itchy red rash.
beats.caption: Wedding morning, an itchy rash appears

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Don't panic, let me grind up some plain oats for a quick bath soak.
beats.caption: "A quick oatmeal soak will help"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: We're an hour from the ceremony and you're already thinking oatmeal. Classic. Is this one real?
beats.caption: "Is oatmeal even real medicine?"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Compounds in oats called avenanthramides calm inflammation and itching. It's actually an FDA-recognized skin protectant, not just folklore.
beats.caption: Oats are FDA-recognized for skin

factReveal.citation: Avenanthramides in colloidal oatmeal reduce inflammation and itch; recognized as an effective skin protectant in dermatology research

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Four for four. I'm a little proud of myself right now.
beats.caption: 4/4! All four remedies checked out

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Don't get too proud yet. Not every home remedy gets off this easy.
beats.caption: But not every remedy gets off this easy

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The ceremony went off without a hitch. Everyone was healthy, the rash long gone.
beats.caption: The ceremony goes off perfectly

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: See? Old remedies, still holding up just fine.
beats.caption: "Old remedies still hold up"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: I'll give you that. But apple cider vinegar for digestion, or Epsom salt for sore muscles? The actual evidence there is pretty thin, mostly just word of mouth.
beats.caption: ACV and Epsom salt: pretty thin evidence

factReveal.citation: Current evidence for apple cider vinegar improving digestion and for magnesium absorption through Epsom salt baths remains weak, largely anecdotal

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: That's exactly why I need a nursing-school granddaughter, to sort out which ones to trust.
beats.caption: "Need you to sort out which to trust"

beats.speaker: granddaughter
beats.text: Folk wisdom is genuinely worth something, but double-check it against real science, and see an actual doctor for anything serious.
beats.caption: Double-check it. See a doctor if serious.

beats.speaker: grandma
beats.text: Follow along for more of us fact-checking home remedies. Maybe your family's favorite trick is next.
beats.caption: Follow for more fact-checked remedies
